findings.text: Classic low resolution timer object keeps frequently mutated runtime state together for cache locality. It carries a hash linkage used for wheel or bucket placement, a tick count marking expiry, a callback that receives the address of the object itself, and flag bits. A lock validation map is present only when that debugging option is enabled.

Ordered expiry queues use red black tree nodes keyed by a monotonic time value. The plain node pairs a tree link with an expiry stamp and its head holds a cached tree root for fast minimum lookup. The linked variant pairs an intrusive linked tree node with an expiry stamp and its head holds a linked tree root supporting predecessor and successor traversal.

Queue membership is a two state lifecycle. Initialization puts a node into the detached state by clearing its tree link. Insertion moves it to queued. Removal returns it to detached. A predicate reports queued by testing whether the link is non empty, so callers must initialize before first use and must not assume detachment implies a valid expiry.

Plain expiry queue offers minimum peek, node preparation, membership test and head preparation. Peek returns the container of the leftmost cached entry or a null safe empty result when the queue is empty. Preparation clears a node, membership reports whether it is currently linked, and head preparation installs an empty cached root.

Linked expiry queue offers first, next, previous, delete and preparation helpers. First inspects the cached leftmost slot, next and previous walk the intrusive links from a given node, all with null safe container translation. Delete unlinks a node and reports whether it had been present. Preparation clears a node or installs an empty linked root and membership is tested through link emptiness.

Timer file descriptor control flags use bit zero for absolute expiry and bit one for cancel on clock change. Close on exec and nonblocking file options are shared between creation and general handling. Creation accepts only that shared file pair, while arming accepts only the absolute and cancel on change pair. A write ioctl with magic T on index zero carries a tick count width value.

Clock identifiers are small sequential integers starting at zero for realtime, then one for monotonic, two and three for process and thread CPU time, four for raw monotonic, five and six for coarse realtime and coarse monotonic, seven for boottime, eight and nine for realtime and boottime alarms, ten for SGI cycle and eleven for TAI. Total base slots are sixteen, auxiliary clocks start at sixteen with eight slots ending at twenty three. Interval timers are zero for real, one for virtual and two for profile. Absolute timer option is one.

User time values separate seconds from sub second parts. Legacy timespec pairs old seconds with nanoseconds, timeval pairs old seconds with microseconds, and interval forms pair a period with a current value. Timezone holds minutes west plus daylight type. Process times hold user, system and waited child user and system tick counts. Modern kernel forms use 64 bit seconds with 64 bit sub second parts, while old and socket variants preserve narrower layouts for compatibility.

NTP control block carries a mode selector, offset, frequency, maximum and estimated errors, status word, time constant, precision, tolerance, current time, tick length, PPS frequency and jitter, shift duration, stability and several PPS counters, plus TAI offset and trailing padding. A wide kernel variant preserves the same logical order with 64 bit fields and explicit 32 bit pads, using a 64 bit seconds plus microseconds time member.

NTP API version is four. Mode bits select offset, frequency, maximum error, estimated error, status, time constant, TAI, set offset, microsecond, nanosecond and tick behaviors, with historic aliases equating mode names to adjust names. Status bits distinguish PLL, PPS frequency and time, frequency lock, leap insert and delete, unsynchronized, frequency hold, PPS signal conditions, hardware fault, resolution, mode and clock source, with a read only aggregate covering signal, fault, resolution, mode and source bits. Leap and sync reports run zero through five for ok, insert, delete, in progress, wait and error, with bad aliasing error.

NTP scaling uses shift two for PLL and FLL factors, maximum time constant ten, microsecond shift sixteen, scale shift thirty two, inverse shift nineteen, maximum phase error five hundred million nanoseconds, maximum frequency error five hundred thousand, minimum update interval two hundred fifty six seconds and maximum two thousand forty eight seconds. Tick frequency equals HZ with interval length derived from seconds per second divided by that frequency. Legacy timer tick rate is 1193182.

Right shift helper preserves sign by negating, shifting magnitude, then reapplying sign for negative inputs while shifting directly for non negative inputs, using the operand types. Entropy helper has two builds, one reading CPU cycle counter and broadening it to unsigned long, the other delegating to a fallback routine.

Shared time page centers on a clock descriptor with sequence counter, mode selector, last cycle snapshot, optional overflow guard, mask, multiplier, shift and per base timestamps. Each timestamp pairs seconds with nanoseconds. The same storage is overlaid with namespace offsets when time namespaces are active. Top level page adds architecture data, two base clocks for high resolution plus coarse and raw, auxiliary clocks, timezone fields, high resolution timer granularity and padding, aligned to cache line. Random page holds a generation counter plus readiness flag. Architecture data defaults to empty or a placeholder byte.

Shared page distinguishes TAI plus one bases, with high resolution covering realtime, monotonic, boottime and TAI, coarse covering both coarse clocks, raw covering raw monotonic, and auxiliary covering a contiguous mask from first to last auxiliary clock. Clock storage uses index zero for shared high resolution and coarse and index one for raw, for two bases. Page order is time, time namespace, random, then architecture pages, with architecture size rounded up to page granularity. Linker symbols for random and architecture pages are either provided at fixed page offsets or left empty depending on build.

Clock mode enumeration starts at none, allows architecture inserted values, ends at a maximum sentinel, and reserves the largest signed integer to mark time namespace views. Auxiliary clock granularity is fixed at one nanosecond. Cache line size follows level one size and alignment helpers round addresses up or down to a given power of two boundary, including pointer forms. Constant helpers wrap long and long long literal construction.

Tracing provides symbolic decoders for diagnostics. Timer flags decode migrating, deferrable, pinned and irq safe bits. Clock decoder covers realtime, monotonic, boottime and TAI. High resolution timer mode decoder covers absolute versus relative combined with pinned, soft and hard qualifiers. Soft interrupt decoder covers ten classes from high priority through RCU. Tick dependency decoder covers none plus POSIX timer, perf, scheduler, unstable clock, RCU and RCU expedited causes. Each family has an enum definition form and a value to string form.

Classic timer carries an optional lock dependency map used to validate callback locking discipline when that checker is enabled. Shared clock descriptor starts with a sequence counter intended to let readers detect concurrent writer updates and retry, separating torn reads from stable snapshots.

Peek helpers return null when empty so callers must check before dereferencing. Membership state is inferred only from link emptiness, so uninitialized storage can falsely appear queued. Coarse, raw, high resolution and auxiliary clock sets must not be confused because they index different storage. Status read only bits and leap states must be treated as observed state rather than commands.
Auxiliary clock granularity query is an always inline leaf returning a constant one nanosecond resolution, usable from shared library contexts without entering the kernel.
